Requirements/Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering

Requirement · critical criticality

Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering

Render user- or model-supplied HTML safely. Inputs include LLM output, pasted content and stored rich text. The sanitizer must remove scripts, event handlers, dangerous URL schemes and mutation-XSS vectors while preserving the formatting we allow.

Owner: platform-securityCadence: 90 daysCreated 27 Oct 20267 candidates
Decision ApprovedActive

Adopt dompurify

Browser-first sanitizer and the de facto standard. It parses untrusted HTML with the same DOM the browser will use, which is why it holds up against mutation XSS. One dependency, 11.7 KB gzip, 45M weekly downloads, and zero executions in our 25-vector browser harness. The gap is release integrity: npm publishes are manual and the tarball is unattested, although the release artifacts are SLSA-attested and Sigstore-signed and the shipped dist files match those hashes.

Build vs buy scores the capability, not this package. A rejected package can still be a capability worth buying from a maintained alternative.

Constraints

  • Removes scripts, event handlers and javascript:/data: URLs
  • Resistant to mutation XSS when the output is re-parsed
  • Actively maintained with a public security process
  • Zero or small dependency tree
  • Runs where it is needed: browser DOM or Node
  • TypeScript types available

Out of scope

  • Markdown authoring
  • Content Security Policy
  • URL allowlisting beyond scheme checks

Decision rationale

Use DOMPurify wherever a browser DOM is available, because parsing with the real DOM is the strongest defence against mutation XSS. Use sanitize-html for Node and SSR, where jsdom would add 27 MB for the same outcome. Use rehype-sanitize when content already flows through remark/rehype, which is the case for the assistant-ui react-markdown pipeline. Keep isomorphic-dompurify on hold: it is correct, but only worth its jsdom footprint if you need DOMPurify specifically on the server. Keep xss on hold: it is fast and safe in the harness, but its escape-not-strip model and lack of independent advisory coverage make it a weaker default. insane and sanitizer are abandoned and must not be used. No package in this category publishes npm provenance, so pin exact versions, subscribe to advisories for the chosen sanitizer, and re-review every 90 days. A 25-vector headless-Chrome corpus executed 11 vectors unsanitized and zero after every tested sanitizer.

Review timeline

  1. 27 Oct 2026 sanitizer Avoid Google Caja's HTML sanitizer, last released in 2015. Zero dependencies, but abandoned for a decade and unsuitable for a security-critical path.
  2. 27 Oct 2026 insane Avoid Abandoned since 2016 and carries an unfixed ReDoS advisory. Do not use for untrusted input.
  3. 27 Oct 2026 xss Hold Active whitelist sanitizer that HTML-escapes disallowed tags rather than stripping them, so blocked markup appears as visible text. Fast and dependency-light, but it has no independent advisory history and 70 open issues.
  4. 27 Oct 2026 isomorphic-dompurify Hold Convenience wrapper that runs DOMPurify on jsdom for server-side use. Output matches DOMPurify, but it pulls 27 MB and 28 packages and inherits jsdom's exposure. Use only if you specifically need DOMPurify on the server.
  5. 27 Oct 2026 rehype-sanitize Adopt The right choice if content already flows through remark/rehype: it sanitizes the HAST tree against an explicit schema instead of round-tripping through the DOM. Zero advisories, tiny and type-safe, but no release since 2023 and a small community.
  6. 27 Oct 2026 sanitize-html Adopt Server-first parser sanitizer. Faster than DOMPurify-on-jsdom and far lighter than dragging in jsdom, but its defaults are aggressive: img and svg are removed unless you allow them. Zero executions in the harness; 17 historical advisories, all fixed, and the current release is clean.
  7. 27 Oct 2026 dompurify Adopt Browser-first sanitizer and the de facto standard. It parses untrusted HTML with the same DOM the browser will use, which is why it holds up against mutation XSS. One dependency, 11.7 KB gzip, 45M weekly downloads, and zero executions in our 25-vector browser harness. The gap is release integrity: npm publishes are manual and the tarball is unattested, although the release artifacts are SLSA-attested and Sigstore-signed and the shipped dist files match those hashes.
